# Multi-Planet Logistics — Running a 9-Planet Empire

Fetched by hand from the live page after a search for empire-management material, because the
community wiki keeps colony placement and empire logistics thin. The doctrine below is what a
player does with nine planets; the figures describe that project's own speed servers, so treat them
as illustrations of a rule, never as host values.

## Stated technique (verbatim)

- Every planet has a job. Define what each world produces or builds before you place a single mine. Some planets mine Metal, some mine Crystal, one or two specialize in Deuterium for fuel, and your main world (or a dedicated shipyard world) builds the ships and defenses your fleet needs.
- Resources must move, not sit. Mines generate resources continuously; storage eventually caps out. A planet that hits storage cap is a mine that has stopped working. Your cargo network exists to prevent that.
- Build queues are assets, not afterthoughts. Each idle build slot is opportunity cost measured in ships not built.
- Most players discover the logistics wall the same way: they colonize their fifth or sixth planet, slap mines on it, and then completely forget about it for three days. When they finally check back, the planet has a storage full of Metal and an empty build queue. That is not an empire — that is a collection of mining camps with no manager.
- The most reliable empire architecture is hub-and-spoke. One or two central hub planets receive raw resources from outlying spoke planets, process them into build orders, and dispatch finished goods (ships, defenses) or construction credits across the empire. Every other planet has a clear role and a clear destination for its surplus.
- Your hub should sit in the geographic center of your empire footprint — ideally in the middle galaxy of your colonization spread, close to the system your moon sits in. Centrality minimizes Deuterium burn on cargo hops.
- Hub planets typically carry your highest-level Robotics Factory, Nanite Factory (if you have it), and Shipyard. They build ships. They do not mine. Their Metal and Crystal mines can stay low because raw ore arrives by freighter from the spoke worlds.
- Metal/Crystal producers: Max Metal Mine and Crystal Mine, moderate Fusion Reactor or Solar Plant, Deuterium Synthesizer only high enough to fuel local cargo hops. Storage levels should match roughly 18-24 hours of production at your chosen dispatch frequency.
- Deuterium farms: High Deuterium Synthesizer, positioned in galaxies 4-6 where planet temperatures run lower (cooler planets get a production bonus on Deuterium). These planets fund your entire cargo and combat fuel budget.
- A common 9-planet split for a mature empire: one hub, four Metal/Crystal spokes, two Deuterium farms, one secondary shipyard, one research world (or the hub doubles as research world once Intergalactic Research Network is up).
- Size your Large Cargo fleet per route based on one simple rule: arrive before the storage would overflow. If a planet produces 500,000 Metal per hour and your Level 10 storage holds 5,400,000, dispatch before the six hours are up — or upgrade storage. Letting storage cap is the single most common reason empires underperform their mine levels.
- The two-queue minimum rule: Never let a planet's build queue go empty without having a reason. If you log in and a planet has an empty queue, that is an alarm, not a normal state. The practical way to enforce this: before you log out, mentally walk every planet from slot 1 to slot 9 and confirm each shipyard or construction queue has at least 24 hours of work queued.
- Not every planet needs to build every ship type. Specialization speeds throughput because you can level each planet's Shipyard and Nanite Factory to match what it builds. A planet dedicated to building Recyclers and Large Cargos needs a Level 10-12 Shipyard and a Nanite Factory — that is it. Your combat ship planet needs the highest Shipyard level possible and should receive resources as a priority, because Battleships and Destroyers cost far more per unit than utility ships.
- Counter-intuitively, a disciplined empire builder can out-pace an active raider on total fleet points simply by keeping queues full. When you are online, raid. When you are logging off, fill every queue.
- Within a single galaxy, Large Cargos (LC) are almost always the right choice for empire logistics. Their cargo capacity per unit is five times that of Small Cargos (SC), and their Deuterium consumption per 1,000 cargo capacity is lower on runs of more than a few systems. Small Cargos shine for rapid-reaction moves — grabbing debris fields, quick same-system transfers.
- A simple sizing formula: calculate peak daily production on each spoke planet, divide by your intended daily dispatch count, then size your LC stack to move that volume in one trip with 10-20% buffer for raided resources you want to forward to safety.
- Consolidate trips. If two spoke planets are in adjacent systems, route one LC fleet through both before returning to the hub. Multi-stop routes cost marginally more flight time but dramatically less total Deuterium per unit of cargo moved.
- A common mistake: players fleetsave their combat fleet and leave their cargo fleet on planets overnight. A 50-LC fleet sitting on a planet is an attractive target. Either park your cargo fleets in flight (deploy to a planet or moon as a fleetsave), fold them into your main fleetsave, or — if the cargo fleet is modestly sized — keep them behind moon cover.
- OGame's Empire View is the most underused tool in the average player's arsenal. It gives you a real-time snapshot of every planet's resources, production rates, building levels, and fleet positions on a single scrollable screen.
- On login, open the Empire View and check three things in order: Storage warnings. Any planet where resource bars are near capacity needs an immediate dispatch or a storage upgrade queued... Empty build queues. Any planet showing no ongoing construction is an idle factory... Fleet positions. Confirm your combat and cargo fleets are where you left them.
- IRN is one of the most impactful technologies for empire operators. It allows your highest-level Research Lab on any planet to benefit from the combined lab levels across your entire empire (up to the IRN level cap). Build IRN early and keep spoke planet labs leveled.
- As your tech levels rise and your fleet compositions change, the optimal planet specialization shifts. A planet that was a Metal producer at Month 1 might be better converted to a secondary shipyard at Month 3. Run the Empire View numbers and rebalance proactively rather than reacting when a bottleneck becomes painful.
- Start thinking about logistics at your third or fourth planet. By the time you have four colonies, the resource imbalance between planets becomes difficult to manage without a system. Define planet roles and cargo routes early — it is far easier to expand a working system than to retrofit one onto chaos.
- Not on every planet, but on any planet with a dedicated Shipyard role, yes. [Nanite Factory] ... For pure mining planets that never build ships, a Nanite Factory is wasted resources. Keep Nanite Factories on your hub and any secondary shipyard worlds only.
